Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark, Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person

Vignette:
Boun is seventy-seven years old, a man whose life has been shaped by two vastly different kinds of fire. For the last forty years, he has been a firefighter in a quiet American suburb, a job of controlled risk and civic duty. But the fires that burn in his mind are from a lifetime ago, from a war that history books barely mention. He has carried the memories from his village in Laos for over fifty years, and with his retirement approaching, the carefully constructed walls he built around them are beginning to crumble.

The event itself returns to him not as a coherent story, but in fragments of sensory horror. He was a young man, not yet twenty, helping his father mend a fishing net in the afternoon sun. There was no warning, just a high-pitched whistle that grew into a deafening roar. The world became a storm of dirt and splintered wood. When the shaking stopped, the air was thick with dust and the smell of cordite. He remembers the silence that came first, a ringing void, and then the screaming. He found his friend, Sida, near the riverbank, or what was left of him. Boun can still see the vibrant yellow of Sida’s shirt, now stained crimson and coated in grey dust. He remembers the frantic, desperate sounds that followed – not the clean, piercing sirens of his American fire engine, but the sputtering engines of old trucks and carts being used as makeshift ambulances, their horns bleating uselessly against the scale of the devastation.

These fragments force their way into his present. The memory is so vivid, so detailed, that it feels entirely separate from the life he has built. It does not feel like something that happened to him, the respected firefighter and grandfather; it feels like a film he was forced to watch, an experience so alien it must belong to someone else. Yet it intrudes without permission. A few weeks ago, during a routine drill at the station, a trainee set off a small, controlled explosive to simulate a backdraft. The sudden, sharp bang sent Boun stumbling backwards, his mind instantly filled with the image of Sida’s yellow shirt. For a moment, he was not in the concrete training yard but back in the ruins of his village, a terrified boy again. He covered it with a gruff comment about his old ears, but the shame was hot and immediate. He felt like an object, a piece of old machinery that had malfunctioned, not a person in control.

His life has become a series of negotiations with his own mind. He constantly scans his surroundings, a habit he can’t break. In the supermarket, he tracks the exits, notes who comes and goes, a low-level thrum of anxiety that leaves him perpetually exhausted. His wife has noticed him calling out names in his sleep, names from a life she has only ever heard about in brief, clipped sentences. Hearing a name even vaguely similar to Sida’s on the television or radio can stop him in his tracks. To manage the terror, he has developed silent rituals. He avoids going to bed until he is on the verge of collapse, often staying up until two or three in the morning watching old movies. The dark and quiet of the bedroom is an invitation for the memories to flood in. In those late hours, he sometimes finds himself lost in elaborate fantasies of revenge, imagining himself tracking down the pilots who dropped the bombs, a fleeting and bitter taste of power in a life that began with absolute powerlessness.

He has long been certain that if he were to truly allow himself to think about what happened, to feel the full weight of it, he would simply shatter. He carries a deep, unshakeable belief that a better man, a stronger man, would have done something different—run faster, hidden sooner, saved someone. This self-reproach has shadowed him across decades and an ocean. It was his wife who finally insisted he seek help. She found him one morning in the kitchen, staring blankly at the wall, having not slept at all. He had been woken by the sound of a distant ambulance and couldn't shake the image of the sputtering trucks. Boun is here now not with hope, but with a quiet desperation. He is terrified of what opening this door might unleash, but the idea of living out his final years as a prisoner to the ghost of a boy in a yellow shirt is a greater fear still.
